description:
A group of Aerospace Engineering Students from Universiti Putra Malaysia. We are passionate about space, technology and using our skills to solve real-world engineering problems. 

We aim to learn and deepen our understanding of coding skills and engineering challenges faced in space through this NASA Space APP Challenge 2026.
summary: We developed a game to simulate a space craft landing on the moon. We included different difficulty or variables so players can have fun while learning  the different factors that affect a moon landing. Through this game, we successfully simplified the existing tools by determining Sun and Earth positions to search for the most suitable candidate landing sites.
details:
LUNE: Mission Control is a browser-based educational game developed to simplify lunar landing site evaluation, particularly around the Moon's south pole. Players select one of three landing sites, adjust their landing date, and evaluate sunlight availability, Earth visibility, and battery performance. Each mission presents three objectives, encouraging players to experiment with different scenarios before launching a simulation. An Endless Expedition mode also generates additional challenges with varying requirements.

Our project uses precomputed data from NASA's JPL Horizons system, including Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation measurements at 30-minute intervals. Python was used to retrieve and process these datasets, while HTML, CSS, and JavaScript were used to develop the game interface, simulations, and scoring system. Visual Studio Code and browser development tools supported testing and debugging, alongside AI-assisted development tools such as Claude and ChatGPT.

As aerospace engineering students, our team wanted to make complex mission-planning concepts understandable to people without technical backgrounds. We incorporated interactive visualizations, a robotic assistant named HALO, and a mission-based reward system to make learning more engaging. Feedback from participants also helped us improve objective clarity and gameplay interactions.

Our intended impact is to encourage younger audiences to explore aerospace engineering through interactive problem-solving. By combining NASA-derived data with accessible gameplay, LUNE demonstrates how landing dates and locations influence spacecraft operations. The current prototype uses a simplified geometric horizon and educational battery model, making it suitable for learning rather than actual mission certification.
